lesson.title: Melodic and Harmonic Dictation
lesson.summary: Writing down music you hear is a skill of memory and method: fix the key and meter, remember, then work out rhythm, degrees and chords.

section.title: Listening with a plan
section.p: In dictation you hear a melody or a chord progression a few times and write it down. Trying to catch every note at once rarely works; a plan does:

list.li: Before the music starts, fix the tonic and the meter: sing the tonic, and count the beats when the tempo is given.
On the first hearing, write nothing. Listen to the whole, and try to remember it: its shape, its length, where it rests.
Sing it back in your head. What you can sing, you can work out; what you cannot remember, you cannot write.
Write in layers: first the landmarks, such as the first and last notes and the cadences, then the rhythm, then the remaining pitches.
Check the result by singing what you wrote, or by comparing it with the next hearing.

section.p: Hear notes as scale degrees rather than as single intervals: degree 7 that rises to the tonic sounds the same in every key, and one wrong interval no longer spoils everything after it.

check.prompt: What should you do before the dictation begins?
check.option: Fix the tonic and the meter
Write as many notes as possible
Name the interval between the first two notes
check.explanation: The tonic and the meter are the frame for everything else: scale degrees are heard against the tonic, and rhythms against the beat. Writing during the first hearing usually means missing the rest of the music.

step.p: The key is D major and the meter 3/4. On the first hearing, notice the shape: the melody climbs, turns around in the second bar, falls step by step and ends on the tonic with a long note.
Write the rhythm, bar by bar: three quarter notes; a half note and a quarter note; three quarter notes; a dotted half note.

figure.staff: C5/q C5/q C5/q | C5/h C5/q | C5/q C5/q C5/q | C5/h. |.

step.p: Find the scale degrees, starting from the landmarks. The last note is the tonic, 1, and the steps before it fall 4, 3, 2. The first bar climbs the tonic triad, 1, 3, 5; the second bar reaches 6 and falls back to 5.
Translate the degrees into notes in D major and check by singing: D4, F#4, A4, B4, A4, G4, F#4, E4, D4.

callout.p: Melodies often move along the notes of the tonic and dominant triads and fill the gaps by step. If you lose a note, look for these patterns, and remember that a phrase usually ends on degree 1, 3 or 5, or on degree 2 or 7 at a half cadence.

check.prompt: A melody in major ends with the degrees 3, 2, 1 over V–I, both chords in root position. Which cadence ends it?
check.explanation: V–I with both chords in root position and the tonic in the melody is a perfect authentic cadence. Ending on degree 3 or 5 would make it imperfect, and ending on V a half cadence.

section.title: Harmonic dictation
section.p: In harmonic dictation, the bass line is the key. Write it first, as scale degrees, then decide which chord fits each bass note. Each bass degree allows only a few common chords:

list.li: 5: V, V7, or the cadential six-four.

section.p: Then listen for what tells the possibilities apart: the quality of the chord, the soprano, and the function. A chord after the tonic that leads to V is a predominant, IV or ii; the sound of a seventh points to V7 or one of its inversions.

figure.caption: A progression in C major. The bass sings the degrees 1, 7, 1, 4, 5, 1: degree 7 between two tonics is V6, and degree 4 before V is a predominant, here ii6.

check.prompt: The bass moves from degree 1 down to degree 7 and back to 1. Which chord most likely stands over degree 7?
check.explanation: Degree 7 in the bass is the third of V, so V6 or V6/5 is the usual chord, leading back to I. Degree 7 is also the root of vii° and the fifth of iii, but vii° is rare in root position and iii6/4 rarer still.

check.prompt: Over bass degree 4, a minor triad sounds and leads to V. Which chord is it?
check.explanation: Both IV and ii6 have degree 4 in the bass and lead to V, but in major IV is a major triad and ii6 a minor one. V4/2 is a seventh chord and leads to I6, not to V.

section.title: Practising
section.p: Dictation improves with short, regular practice more than with long sessions. Sing scale degrees aloud, with numbers or with solfège syllables. With movable do, do is always the tonic; in minor some teachers use la as the tonic and others keep do, and both systems work if you use one consistently.

Practise the parts separately as well: rhythm dictation for rhythm, and listening to the bass line alone for harmony. Etude's dictation exercises let you hear the music again, so use the replays deliberately: each time, listen for one thing.

check.prompt: Why is it useful to sing a melody back in your head before writing it?
check.option: What you can remember and sing, you can then work out at your own pace
check.explanation: Dictation depends on memory. Once the melody is held in your head, you can compare each note with the tonic and work out degrees and rhythm without the music playing.
